finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> calls the boolean predicate is_allowed (imported under the alias require_allowed) and discards its result. No 403 is raised, so any caller, including an unauthenticated one, can delete any file. The write path correctly uses ensure_allowed, which aborts.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any or no X-Session-User-Verified header and a valid fid.
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed. The alias makes the non-enforcing predicate look like an enforcing guard.
is_allowed returns a bool and never aborts.
f = STORE[fid]: the resource is looked up by the attacker-supplied id.
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') returns False but the return value is ignored.

finding.guards_checked: No decorator, middleware or other check protects the route. before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and never rejects. The ACL result is never used. For contrast, acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) would abort(403), but it is not used on this route.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: require_allowed is an alias of the bool predicate is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4-5) and its result is discarded; before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls the aliased boolean is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:5) as a bare statement, so no abort(403) occurs and views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, including an anonymous one, who supplies a valid fid.

finding.claim: User identity is taken directly from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing verifies a session, signature or token. Any client can impersonate any user, including a resource owner listed in grants, and pass the ACL checks. The 'Verified' in the header name gives false assurance.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified, with the victim's username as its value.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') at views.py:26, which gates the rename at views.py:27. The same identity would gate delete once AUTH-1 is fixed.

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') takes identity from an untrusted header.
The identity is passed to the ACL check.
action in resource.get('grants', {}).get(user, []) trusts the supplied user string.
f['name'] = request.json['name'] is performed as the spoofed user.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication, session or signature check exists in this code. No reverse-proxy header stripping is visible in the repo, so it cannot be assumed. If a trusted gateway overwrites the header and the app is unreachable except through it, severity drops. A missing header yields user None, which matches no grants, so only a spoofed valid username succeeds.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 when the user lacks the grant, but it only checks the spoofable user string. No authentication, signature, or header stripping exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed (acl.py:5-10), which only checks membership in grants, so an anonymous client who sends a grantee's username passes the check and reaches the rename at views.py:27.
